newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed around intra-day lows at the end of the session as earlier weakness predominated after selling in New York, traders said. Activity on the London market was described as lackluster by market players, anxious to square their positions before the extended weekend. The LCE will be closed on Monday due to a public holiday.

At the close November stood $28 lower on the day at $1,667 a tonne and all other traded positions were lower. Switch activity was concentrated in September and November. Nearby tightness in New York is seen stirring the market higher in the coming days. The November contract was expected to trade sideways in the medium turn, but move higher on a short-term basis. Resistance was pegged in a band between $1,700 and $1,800 with nearby support at $1,590.

Arabica futures in New York ended moderately higher as a late round of fund buying erased earlier losses and lifted the December contract to a fresh three months' high, traders said. Origin selling and local profit taking pressured values from the outset, but after the most active December contract survived a test of 118.00 cents/lb support, dealers said downward momentum came to a halt.

Benchmark December coffee closed up 1.75 cents, at 122.55 cents while front month September ended up 1.15 cents/lb, at 132.25 cents. The remaining months gained 0.05 to 2.10 cents. Market sources noted that there were still no delivery notices issued against the spot September contract, and although September's open interest continued to decline, exchange warehouses hold a meager 34,516 bags of coffee. Therefore some analysts believe the tight delivery situation will continue.

NICARAGUA - USDA recently reported that its field office in San Jose, Costa Rica, has cut its estimate of 1995/96 and 1996/97 Nicaraguan coffee production due to abnormal rainfall. In its world agricultural production report, USDA said the San Jose office now pegs the 1996/97 Nicaraguan crop at 680,000 bags, down 15 per cent from a preliminary forecast in June of 800,000. Additionally, the 1995/96 estimate has been cut 27 per cent from 920,000 bags to 676,000, USDA said.

Nicaraguan producers are also still plagued by a spread of coffee rust, which has affected more than 20 per cent of Nicaragua's coffee trees, USDA said. The fungus has been in Nicaragua since the 1970s and was considered under control until recently, when costs to control the coffee rust began to rise, USDA added. Farmers since have been unable to purchase the necessary fungicides and unseasonably wet weather has led to the spread of the fungus, USDA said.

COLOMBIA - Colombia's National Coffee Growers Federation said it closed registrations for August shipments by private exporters on Friday, August 23. Registrations for August shipment by private exporters had remained open since June 21. The Federation closed August registrations for itself on August 12.

BRAZIL - Coffee exports in May 1996 amounted to 887,175 bags, down from last year's 1.20 million bags. This brought cumulative exports in the first two months of the 1996/97 campaign (April/May) up to 1.61 million bags, sharply down from last year's 2.36 million bags.

Total exports in 1995/96 amounted to 13.66 million bags against 15.84 million bags in 1994/95. Major outlets for green coffee in April/May 1996 were Italy (167,300 vs 335,900 bags), Japan (161,500 vs 192,500 bags) and Argentina (115,000 vs 81,600 bags). The major markets for Brazilian solubles in April/May 1996 were Russia (102,600 vs 92,500 bags) and the USA (92,300 vs 35,100 bags).
